 5. The plaintiffs filed another suit being Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 in the same Court on the same date against the same defendants claiming the right of preemption on the same ground as stated in title Suit No. 100 of 1997. 

 6. Both the suits were contested by defendant No.1 Company purchaser by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the suits were malafide, fraudulent, misconceived and were not maintainable in their present form. The suit land was not liable to be preempted under the Muhammedan Law as the same was neither house nor garden nor a small piece of land. Aground of limitation was also taken in the written statements and it was specifically asserted that Talab-I-Muwasibat and Talab-I-Ishhad had not been property performed in accordance with the Muhammedan Law. Both the suit lands and the 'B' scheduled land had boundary walls on all sides having only one entrance gate on the eastern boundary wall by the said of the public road known as Kashimpur Road. Neither on 09.03.1997 nor on any other date, plaintiff No.2 with M/s. Ershad Hossain and Md. Ismail Meah passed through or could pass through the suit land as it was surrounded on all sides by a through or could pass through the suit land as it was surrounded on all sides by a boundary wall and had a gate on the eastern side which led to Kashimpur Road and therefore, it was not possible for plaintiff No. 2 or anybody else to enter into or pass through the suit land except through the main entrance gate on the northern side of the eastern wall and the gate remained closed under the supervision of security guard and nobody could enter into the suit land without permission and assistance of the employees and security guards of defendant No. 1 Abu Bakar Siddique was not present in the suit land on 09.03.1997 as he was on leave for one mother from 25.02.1997. The plaintiffs and their men were aware of all the developments from the time of negation between defendant Nos. 1 and 2 for sale and execution of the agreement, construction of C.I. sheet but and semi pucca toilets for the employees, execution of tripartite agreement and registration of the sale deeds on 07.03.1996 and M/s. V.K. Ltd. installed and fixed signboard on the eastern wall and installed electric and telephone connection in the suit land on their purchase on 07.03.1996. The lands allegedly purchased by the plaintiffs were bounded on all sides by pucca boundary wall and they were carrying on their manufacturing works therein conveniently and without any inconvenience or difficulty. The suit land was purchased by defendant No.2 from different owners with a view to set up an industry thereon and took loan by mortgaging the land with Sonali Bank and on their failure to repay the loan amount, the bank instituted Mortgage Suit No. 139 of 1990 in Artha Rin Adalat and as defendant No. 2 had no other means to liquidate the liability of the Bank, it entered into an agreement for sale with defendant No.1 and Sonali Bank and ultimately, the entire land was transferred to defendant No.1 through different sale deeds pursuant to the agreement within the knowledge of the plaintiffs. Defendant No.1 sold .42 acre land out of north-eastern part of the suit land to one Md. Serajul Islam, defendant No. 3 through registered kabala dated 16.09.1996 and delivered possession thereof to the purchaser and thus they were in possession of 5.08 acres land out of the total suit land. Neither the suit land nor 'B' scheduled land was specified as required under Order VII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and on the count, the suit was also liable to be dismissed. 

 "The learned Counsel appearing for petitioners in the petitioners submits that the present cases involve important question of law including interpretation of several Articles of the Constitution, which are of great public importance, likely to have immense impact on the nation and the society as a whole, that the learned Judges grossly erred in law in holding that Muslim Personal Law of Pre-emption as unconstitutional and offends the provisions of Article 42 of the Constitution, in the face of the fact that section 96(11) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Act No. XXVIII of 1951), which is a protected law by the first Schedule (under Article 47) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and completely turning blind eye to a decision of the Appellate Division in the case reported in 33DLR (AD) 359, This error has vitiated the whole decision and has resulted serious miscarriage of justice, that the learned Judges also erred in opining that the Muslim Law of Pre-emption offends Articles 31 of the Constitution. 

 9. Mr. T. H. Khan, learned Counsel, for the appellants, has reiterated the submissions on which leave was granted. Therefore, we do not restate the submission made by him. 

 17. The High Court Division further found that the plaintiffs were the owners of 2.58 acres land, whereas they instituted the suit to preempt 8.69 acres land as Shafi-I-Jar. The claim of the right of preemption on the ground of vicinage alone will not lie in the case of large estates and was available only when either houses or small holdings was transferred; preemption under the Mohammedan Law was to prevent the inconvenience which might result from the introduction of a disagreeable stranger as a co-partner or as a near neighbor, its object was to prevent possible vexation arising from a disagreeable neighbor. 

 (2) A law made under clause (1) of this article shall provide for the acquisition, nationalization or requisition with compensation and shall fix the amount of compensation or specify the principles on which, and the manner in which, the compensation is to be assessed and paid; but no such law shall be called in question in any court on the ground that any provision of the law in respect of such compensation is not adequate." 

 (2) The State shall not make any law inconsistent with any provisions of this Part, and any law so made shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void. 

 28. The High Court Division observed that the law of pre-emption was not an "Islamic Institution" or "a Quaranik Law." However, as stated hereinbefore, the High Court Division observed that the concept of pre-emption on the vicinage was based on the saying of the great Prophet (saw) "Neighbour has a right superior to that of a stranger in the land adjacent to him." So, naturally, a question arises what is the status of the saying of great Prophet (was) in Islam and its impact amongst the Muslim? To see this, we have to see what Hadith it: 

 From Hadith comes the Sunnah refers to the actions and statements of the Prophet Muhammad (s) as well as tacit approval of the statements and actions of others. The Qur'an and the Prophet Muhammad (s) were sent down by Allah for the benefit of the whole of the mankind for all time. "Sunnath" (literally, a well-trodden path"-i.e., taken as precedent and authority or directive), to which the faith to which the faithful conform in submission to the sanction that Hadith possesses and that legalists, on that ground, can enjoin. 

 The Qur'an tells us the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) has taught not only the Book but also the wisdom (See Qur'an: 96:2; 33:113, etc.) As Imam Shafi'i stated, the wisdom mentioned here is the Sunnah of Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him); so if we were to reject the Hadith, we would be rejecting the Qur'an itself. The Qur'an tells us to obey the Messenger and abide by his decision: [But no, by the Lord, they can have no (real) Faith, until they make the judge in all disputes between them, and find in in their souls no resitance against Thy decisions, but accept them with the fullest conviction.] (Sura An-Nisaa 4:65). 

 34. The question of pre-emption under Mohammedan Law came up for consideration before this Court in the case of Shamsuddin Ahmed @ Tufa Mia and others (supra). In that case while tracing back the history of law of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law, this Court stated that 

 35. From the above quotation, it is clear that the right of preemption under the Mohammedan Law assumed the character of law and in fact, it is stated so in all the books of all the authors of Islamic jurists who have written the Mohammedan Law including Hedaya. 

 37. Mr. Tabarak Hossain, learned Counsel, for the respondent, conceded that the right of preemption under Mohammedan Law on the ground of vicinage as well as on other grounds is practiced in this region, now Bangladesh, right from ancient period as observed by this Division in the above mentioned case. At the risk of repetition, we state that the right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage having emanated from Hadis and having been practiced since from time immemorial in this region has become a law within the meaning of article 152 of the Constitution. Further if we see article 152 of the Constitution and article 42(1) thereof side by side, it would appear that the right to acquire, hold, transfer, or otherwise disposal of property is subject to the right of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law including the one on the of vicinage. 

 39. The other reasons assigned by the High Court Division in the above respect are absolutely beyond the periphery of the fundamental rights and are based on mere surmises and conjectures and based on sound judicial principle and so those are not required to be met by this Court. Moreso, in holding that the right of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law on the ground of vicinage is an unreasonable restriction in acquiring, holding and transferring a property by a citizen, the High Court Division failed to consider that the Muslims of this region have been exercising the right of the pre-emption on the ground of vicinage for centuries and nobody either of the Muslim Community or the Hindu Community of part of the region ever raised any question that the right put unreasonable restrictions in acquiring, holding and transferring a property. In the written statement, on pleading to that respect was also token. The learned Judges themselves also found so, when they observed "It surprises us that neither during the Pakistani days nor even after the emergence of Bangladesh, the constitutionality of pre-emption law in the ground of vicinage has been challenged before this Court." The above fact prima-facie proves that the citizens accepted the right of pre-emption of the Muslims under the Mohammedan Law on the ground of vicinage as the personal law of the Muslims. When the framers of the Constitution in Part III thereof clearly recognized "any restrictions imposed by law" that restrictions must be subject to the law of pre-emption on the vicinage as recognized in the Mohammedan Law. And in deciding the question of reasonable restriction put by law, we must remember that the right of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law is not an act of Parliament and this law has emanated from the Hadis of the Prophet (saw) as discussed earlier which has become part of personal law and that is protected by article 41(1)(a) of the Constitution which has clearly mandated that every citizen has the right of profess, practice or propagate any religion. But the High Court Division totally failed to consider the status of Hadis and its impact in the personal law as envisaged in article 41(1)(a) discussed above. In the context, we must state that the reasonableness to any restriction imposed by law comes only when a law is enacted by the Parliament. In the context, we find it quire appropriate to quote another passage from the Constitutional Law of Mr. Mahmudul Islam. The passage reads thus: 

 "When it is said that substantive due process requires a law to be reasonable, the question arises: reasonable in relation to what? The American Supreme Court evolved that concept of 'police power', which is a short description of the inherent power of the State to promote the general welfare of the community, and judged reasonableness of laws in relation to the police power of the State. But the question still remains as to whose conception of reasonableness is control-that of the legislator or that of the court? "In a very famous footnote in United States V. Caroline Products Co." the court articulated the idea that different constitutional claims be subject to varying levels of review." Rational basis test involves a relaxed scrutiny. Under it a law will be upheld if it is found rationally related to a legitimate government purpose. Intermediate scrutiny involves a deeper scrutiny than rational basis test and under it the law will be held valid if it is substantially related to an important government purpose. The third level of scrutiny is strict scrutiny in which case the government to sustain the validity of a law must show that law is necessary to achieve a compelling government purpose. It is level of scrutiny selected by the court that principally determines the fate of a particular case. If the court applies rational basis test, a law or action is very likely to be found valid, while a case attracting the strict scrutiny, the law or action is most likely to be found invalid as the government can hardly show that the law or action subseries any compelling interest." 

 40. We consider the rational basis test, the most appropriate basis to test the reasonableness of a law and the law of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law on the basis of vicinage is quite rational. As already stated hereinbefore, this law has emanated from the Hadis and being practiced by the Muslims of this part of the region for centuries. Further under the Mohammedan Law, a sale is an exchange of property for property, the exchange consisting in payment of price by the purchaser to the vendor and delivery of possession by the vendor to the purchaser. It is also to be kept in mind that under the Mohammedan Law execution of instrument of sale is not necessary to complete the sale, the sale is complete with the passing of considerations and delivery of possession. And the moment the suit is decreed, the defendants, i.e. the purchaser shall be entitled to get the price of the transferred land, so the right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage is quite rational. Another test of reasonableness of the law is whether the law is arbitrary. The law of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage cannot be said to be arbitrary as well, because if the suit is decreed, the defendant vendee shall get the money back which he paid for the purchase of the property. The right of pre-emption including the one as Shafi-I-Jar having been emanated from the Hadis, every Muslim has the right to practice the same and in Bangladesh, it has always been regarded as a part of personal law, i.e. the Mohammedan Law and that right is guaranteed by article 41(1)(a) of the Constitution to. And the right of pre-emption including the one on the ground of vicinage as recognized in the Mohammedan Law is not inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution and the fundamental rights as guaranteed in Part III of the Constitution. 

 41. The High Court Division was also wrong in holding that the right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage is discriminatory because though a Muslim can exercise the right of pre-emption as Shafi-i-Jar in respect of a non-agricultural land, a Hindu cannot inasmuch the right of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law including the one on the ground of vicinage has become part of personal law as discussed above and such right is protected by article 41(1)(a) of the Constitution. Further the Hindus and the Muslims are two different communities and they form two different classes as well and they follow two different religion and faith. The law of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage having been emanated from the Hadies of the great Prophet (saw) and having been practiced so long cannot be said to be discriminatory. In the context, the High Court Division has totally misread and misconstrued the provisions of article 28 of the Constitution vis-à-vis 41(1)(a) thereof. Further the right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage can be availed of by any Muslim, no discrimination has been made or attempted to have been made by the State between the Muslims. The right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage can be available of by any Muslim irrespective of his status/position in the society. The reasoning of the High Court Division is also fallacious for another reason that so far as the Muslim women of this part of the region are concerned, they inherit from the father whereas, a Hindu woman in this region including Bangladesh does not inherit from the father because of the Hindu Law, i.e. the personal law. So it cannot be said that Hindu Women are being discriminated with the Muslim women. The High Court Division was totally wrong in holding that the right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage "affects the secular nature of the Republic" inasmuch as the State has not made any discrimination against any citizen in availing the right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage between the Muslims and the Hindus, but it is because of the personal law which has been guaranteed in sub-article (1)(a) of article 41 as discussed above. 

 43. From the trend of the impugned judgment, it appears that in holding that the right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage puts an unreasonable restriction upon a citizen in acquiring, holding and transferring a property, the High Court Division relied upon the case of Bhau Ram -Vs- Baij Nath Singh and others heard along with two other appeals, AIR 1962, Supreme Court, 1476 without considering that in the said cases the question of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law on the ground of vicinage was not involved. And in those cases. The constitutionality of certain provisions of the pre-emption laws prevailing in the States of Madya Pradesh (Rewas-State area), Delhi and Maharashtra (Berar area) such as, Rewa State Pre-emption Act, 1946 section 10, in particular, Punjab Pre-emption Act I of 1913, section 16 in particular and section 174 under Chapter XIV of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, were challenged. In those cases, the Supreme Court of India held the statutory or the customary right of pre-emption based on vicinage as unconstitutional on the main ground that before enactment of those laws, there were no practices or customs for pre-emption in those parts of India. Interestingly in the said cases, the Supreme Court upheld the validity of the right of pre-emption based on co-ownership and on certain appendages, such as a common staticase or a common entrance. Regarding vicinage, the Court held that "we are of opinion that even the law of pre-emption creates a right which attaches to property it would be creating a restriction so far acquiring, holding or disposing of property is concerned which was not there before the law of pre-emption was enacted. Therefore, even if the liability attaches to the property, it will still amount to a restriction on the right guaranteed by Art. 19(1)(f), when it attaches to the property by the law of pre-emption." The reason shown in upholding the right of pre-emption on the claim of co-shareship was that though the law giving such a right imposed a reasonable restriction was in the interest of the general public. In the context, it is very pertinent to state that clause (f) of article 19(1) which was interpreted in the above decision, was omitted by the Constitution (44th Amendment) Act, 1978 and the three cases were decided on 7th March, 1962. The High Court Division failed to notice the fact of omission of clause (f) from article 19(1) of the Indian Constitution in 1978. In relying upon this case, the High Court Division also failed to notice the most notorious fact that before enactment of those laws for pre-emption there was no custom or practice of pre-emption in those parts of India whereas, the law of pre-emption under the Muhammedan Law on the ground of vicinage was very much there in Bangladesh for centuries. 

 48. The High Court Division dismissed the suit on the further findings that the right of pre-emption under the Muhammedan Law on the ground of vicinage alone will not lie in the case of large estates and is available only when either houses or small portion of holdings of land are transferred; pre-emption under the Muhammedan Law was to prevent the inconveniences which might result from the introduction of disagreeable stranger as a co-partner or near neighbor, its object being to prevail possible vexation arising from disagreeable neighbor; right of pre-emption, therefore, cannot be enforced in the case of commercial lands. These findings are based on sound judicial principle of law as emanated from the Hadis discussed hereinbefore. In this regard, the High Court Division rightly noticed that in the instant case, the plaintiffs sought pre-emption of the suit land comprising a vast area of 8.69 acres though they were the owners of 2.58 acres land and that the plaintiffs themselves set up industry in 'B' scheduled land. The High Court Division further found that though the suit land was recorded as agricultural land, the admitted position was that in the vicinity of the suit land industrial units were established and that the vendee purchased the suit land for setting up industry. We concur with these findings of the High Court Division and hold that the plaintiffs were not entitled to get the decree in the suit on the ground of vicinage. 

 50. The High Court Division was also correct in holding that the suits were not maintainable inasmuch as after the transfer in question the vendee had already sold .04 acre land to one Serajul Islam who was made defendant No.3 in the suit, but neither in the plaint nor in the deposition of PW 1 any statement was made to the effect that Talib-I-Muwasibat and Talab-I-Ishad were made in respect of the said .40 acre land.
